On the Optimizer Dependence of Neural Scaling Laws

Vansh Ramani* Affiliation:     Shourya Vir Jain* Affiliation:  Affiliation: 
Abstract

The scaling exponent α\alpha in neural scaling laws L⁡(N)∝N−αL(N)\propto N^{-\alpha} is commonly treated as a fixed constant set by architecture and data. We present evidence that α\alpha depends systematically on the optimizer. In controlled random-feature regression experiments—the canonical theoretical framework for neural scaling—we measure α\alpha across five optimizer variants and six spectral conditions. Preconditioned optimizers consistently yield steeper scaling (larger α\alpha), with the α\alpha-shift increasing across most of the tested spectral range, peaking near s=1.5s=1.5, and remaining large at s=2.0s=2.0. At s≈1.0s\approx 1.0 (characteristic of natural language), the full natural gradient achieves α≈0.31\alpha\approx 0.31 versus α≈0.12\alpha\approx 0.12 for gradient descent—a 2.6×2.6\times larger fitted exponent that, within the random-feature model, compounds with each model-size doubling. Whether and how this exponent shift transfers to large-scale LLM training—where recent evidence suggests the advantage may attenuate with scale—remains an important open question. Our results imply that scaling-law forecasts should account for optimizer choice, and we provide a spectral diagnostic predicting when advanced optimizers will pay off.

Accepted at the 4th Workshop on High-dimensional Learning Dynamics (HiLD), ICML 2026.

1 Introduction

Neural scaling laws—the observation that test loss decreases as a power law L⁡(N)∝N−αL(N)\propto N^{-\alpha} with model size NN—govern how frontier laboratories allocate compute (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). The exponent α\alpha determines returns to scaling: larger α\alpha means each doubling of parameters yields greater loss reduction. Current practice treats α\alpha as a fixed constant fit from a few training runs, then extrapolated to set budgets for orders-of-magnitude larger models.

Yet recent results suggest α\alpha may not be fixed. Chen et al. (2025) showed that second-order optimizers—Muon, SOAP (Vyas et al., 2024), and Shampoo (Gupta et al., 2018)—can deliver ∼1.4×\sim\!1.4\times compute speedups over AdamW when their hyperparameters are scaled carefully. Liu et al. (2025) confirmed this at frontier scale: Muon matches AdamW at 52% of training FLOPs. However, the picture is not uniformly positive: Wen et al. (2025) report that the Muon/SOAP speedup over AdamW decays with model size, dropping to ∼1.1×{\sim}1.1\times at 1.2B parameters—suggesting the effect may attenuate at scale. These conflicting findings motivate a more precise question: does Muon improve the constant factor in the scaling law, or does it change the exponent itself? And if the exponent shifts, does the shift persist, shrink, or vanish at scale?

This distinction matters enormously. A constant-factor improvement saves a fixed proportion of compute. An exponent improvement, if it persists, compounds: the advantage grows with every doubling. If preconditioned optimizers change α\alpha—even partially—then forecasts calibrated under AdamW may underestimate returns to scaling under Muon.

We investigate this question in the random-feature regression framework of Maloney et al. (2022) and Bordelon et al. (2024), where data spectrum, optimizer preconditioner, and model capacity can be cleanly isolated. This framework—rooted in the natural gradient theory of Amari (1998) and its modern extensions (Martens, 2020)—lets us study how preconditioning interacts with spectral structure to determine scaling exponents.

Contributions. We make four contributions: (1) the first systematic measurement of α\alpha as a joint function of optimizer type and data spectral decay, across five preconditioner variants and six spectral conditions (Section 3); (2) a mechanistic explanation via an informal proposition: preconditioned optimizers equalize per-mode learning rates, increasing well-learned modes at given NN (Section 2); (3) a comparison to published optimizer-scaling results, treated as qualitative external context rather than a parameter-by-parameter fit (Section 4); and (4) a falsifiable prediction: the α\alpha-shift should generally grow with spectral decay before finite-size or finite-budget saturation; on flat-spectrum data (s<0.3s<0.3), preconditioned optimizers should provide negligible scaling improvement (Section 5).

2 Setup: Random-Feature Regression with Optimizer Preconditioning

2.1 The Random-Feature Scaling Model

We adopt the random-feature regression framework of Maloney et al. (2022), which provides a solvable model for neural scaling laws.

Data distribution. Inputs 𝐱∈ℝD\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} are drawn from 𝒩⁡(0,Σ)\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma) with eigenvalues λi=i−(1+s)\lambda_{i}=i^{-(1+s)}, i=1,…,Di=1,\ldots,D, where s>0s>0 is the spectral exponent. Natural language embeddings typically exhibit s≈0.8​–​1.2s\approx 0.8\text{--}1.2 based on Zipfian frequency distributions (Kaplan et al., 2020; Bahri et al., 2024).

Teacher function. f∗​(𝐱)=∑k=1K∗vk​σ​(𝐰k∗⋅𝐱)f^{*}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{k=1}^{K^{*}}v_{k}\,\sigma(\mathbf{w}^{*}_{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}), with ReLU activation σ\sigma and teacher coefficients vk2∝k−bv_{k}^{2}\propto k^{-b} (source exponent bb).

Student model. y^​(𝐱)=∑j=1Naj​σ​(𝐰j⋅𝐱)\hat{y}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{j=1}^{N}a_{j}\,\sigma(\mathbf{w}_{j}\cdot\mathbf{x}), where {𝐰j}\{\mathbf{w}_{j}\} are fixed random weights from 𝒩⁡(0,ID/D)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{D}/D) and trainable parameters are 𝐚∈ℝN\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. The student minimizes L=𝔼⁡[(y^​(𝐱)−f∗​(𝐱))2]L=\mathbb{E}[(\hat{y}(\mathbf{x})-f^{*}(\mathbf{x}))^{2}].

This produces power-law scaling L⁡(N)∝N−αL(N)\propto N^{-\alpha} where α\alpha depends on ss and bb (Maloney et al., 2022). Crucially, the top-layer problem is a linear regression, allowing different optimizers to be implemented as preconditioners with no confounding from feature learning.

2.2 Optimizer Variants as Preconditioners

We implement five variants, each preconditioning the gradient ∇𝐚L\nabla_{\mathbf{a}}L:

  • •

    GD (baseline): 𝐏=I\mathbf{P}=I.

  • •

    Diagonal (AdamW proxy): 𝐏=diag(𝐅⊤𝐅)−1/2\mathbf{P}=\diag(\mathbf{F}^{\top}\mathbf{F})^{-1/2}.

  • •

    Full NG (Shampoo/K-FAC proxy): 𝐏=(𝐅⊤​𝐅)−1\mathbf{P}=(\mathbf{F}^{\top}\mathbf{F})^{-1}; equivalent to solving the normal equations (Amari, 1998; Martens, 2020).

  • •

    Sign-GD: 𝐚←𝐚−η​sign⁡(∇L)\mathbf{a}\leftarrow\mathbf{a}-\eta\,\sign(\nabla L).

  • •

    Matrix-Sign (Muon proxy): 𝐏=(𝐅⊤𝐅)−1/2\mathbf{P}=(\mathbf{F}^{\top}\mathbf{F})^{-1/2}; equalizes singular values, analogous to Muon’s Newton-Schulz orthogonalization (Jordan, 2024).

Here 𝐅∈ℝn×N\mathbf{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times N} is the random-feature matrix on training data.

2.3 Spectral Intuition: Why Preconditioning Shifts α\alpha

Under GD with power-law data, learning proceeds mode-by-mode from highest variance downward. At model size NN, GD effectively resolves O⁡(Nγ)O(N^{\gamma}) spectral modes for γ<1\gamma<1 set by ss and bb. A preconditioner equalizes convergence rates, rescuing “underserved” low-variance modes. We state this as a spectral argument (not a formal theorem; a fully rigorous proof would require resolvent-trace analysis in the style of Bordelon et al. 2024):

Proposition 1 (Spectral Heuristic—Informal).

Consider random-feature regression with covariance λi∝i−(1+s)\lambda_{i}\propto i^{-(1+s)} and preconditioner 𝐏\mathbf{P}. Let αGD​(s)\alpha_{\textup{GD}}(s) and α𝐏​(s)\alpha_{\mathbf{P}}(s) denote the scaling exponents under GD and preconditioned GD respectively. Heuristically: (i) α𝐏​(s)≥αGD​(s)\alpha_{\mathbf{P}}(s)\geq\alpha_{\textup{GD}}(s) for any positive-definite 𝐏\mathbf{P} that downweights high-variance modes relative to low-variance modes; (ii) the gap Δ​α​(s)=α𝐏​(s)−αGD​(s)\Delta\alpha(s)=\alpha_{\mathbf{P}}(s)-\alpha_{\textup{GD}}(s) is expected to grow with ss until finite-size or finite-budget effects become important; and (iii) Δ​α​(s)→0\Delta\alpha(s)\to 0 as s→0s\to 0 (flat spectrum).

Supporting argument. When 𝐏\mathbf{P} fully inverts the covariance (full NG), every mode converges at the same rate, so all NN capacity units are used uniformly. Under GD, the effective capacity per mode decays with the eigenvalue, so the bottom modes remain under-learned. The fraction of “wasted” capacity grows with spectral steepness ss, making the α\alpha-gap larger. When the spectrum is flat (s→0s\to 0), GD already treats modes equally, so preconditioning adds nothing. Appendix D provides a detailed per-mode convergence-rate derivation supporting all three claims, including explicit convergence factors under GD, full NG, and Matrix-Sign (Equations 2 and 3).

3 Simulation Results

3.1 Experimental Protocol

We fix dimension D=1000D\!=\!1000, teacher complexity K∗=100K^{*}\!=\!100, source exponent b=1.0b\!=\!1.0, and sweep six spectral conditions (ss from 0.250.25 to 2.02.0) and eight model sizes (NN from 2525 to 5,0005{,}000) across all five optimizers. Each configuration uses 10 random seeds, T=2000T\!=\!2000 gradient steps, and optimizer-specific step-size rules (Appendix B). Training set size scales with NN; test set size is 50005000. Scaling exponents are fit by OLS on (log⁡N,log⁡L)(\log N,\log L) for N≥200N\geq 200.

3.2 Core Results

Figure 1 shows the core phenomenon. At s=1.0s=1.0 (panel a), the full natural gradient achieves substantially lower loss at every NN with visibly steeper slope. At s=0.5s=0.5 (panel b), optimizers produce nearly parallel curves.

Figure 2 quantifies the main result. Key patterns:

Preconditioning improves scaling. At every ss, αFullNG>αGD\alpha_{\text{FullNG}}>\alpha_{\text{GD}}, with consistent ordering αFullNG≈αMatSign>αDiag>αSign≈αGD\alpha_{\text{FullNG}}\approx\alpha_{\text{MatSign}}>\alpha_{\text{Diag}}>\alpha_{\text{Sign}}\approx\alpha_{\text{GD}}. Full NG and Matrix-Sign achieve nearly identical α\alpha (e.g., 0.3140.314 vs. 0.3080.308 at s=1.0s=1.0), consistent with both being strong spectral preconditioners.

The α\alpha-shift grows with spectral steepness. At s=0.25s=0.25, Δ​α=0.055\Delta\alpha=0.055; at s=1.0s=1.0, Δ​α=0.195\Delta\alpha=0.195; at s=1.5s=1.5, Δ​α=0.214\Delta\alpha=0.214; and at s=2.0s=2.0, Δ​α=0.191\Delta\alpha=0.191. GD’s exponent collapses as ss grows (αGD\alpha_{\text{GD}}: 0.30→0.010.30\to 0.01), while preconditioned optimizers degrade gracefully (αFullNG\alpha_{\text{FullNG}}: 0.35→0.200.35\to 0.20). This broadly supports Proposition 1, with saturation at the steepest tested spectra.

Effective multiplier is a qualitative comparison. Figure 3 translates the α\alpha-shift into effective compute multipliers. At s≈1.0s\approx 1.0, the random-feature model predicts a substantial parameter-equivalent advantage for strong preconditioners; because this quantity is not a wall-clock or FLOP-normalized speedup, we use published Muon results as directional context rather than a quantitative target.

Table 1 reports full numerical results. Power-law fit quality is high: R2>0.95R^{2}>0.95 for all (optimizer, ss) pairs except Sign-GD at large ss, where the high-variance updates produce noisy scaling (Appendix E).

3.3 Interpretation

The scaling exponent α\alpha measures how efficiently additional capacity reduces loss. Under GD with power-law data, capacity is allocated inefficiently: the optimizer “overspends” on high-variance modes and “underspends” on low-variance modes that still contain signal. A preconditioner corrects this by equalizing effective learning rates. This is not merely a convergence-speed effect—the preconditioner changes the asymptotic relationship between NN and LL because it changes which modes contribute to residual loss at each NN.

4 Validation Against Published Results

The random-feature model omits feature learning, depth, attention, and tokenization, so we treat real-model results as a qualitative check rather than a parameter-by-parameter fit. Chen et al. (2025) studied transformer models from roughly 190M to 1.4B parameters and showed that carefully scaled second-order optimizers, including Muon, SOAP, and Shampoo, can retain about a ∼1.4×{\sim}1.4\times compute advantage over AdamW. That reported Muon advantage is directionally aligned with our finding that, at s≈1.0s\approx 1.0, Matrix-Sign achieves a large positive shift (αMatSign−αGD≈0.19\alpha_{\text{MatSign}}-\alpha_{\text{GD}}\approx 0.19). We do not interpret the random-feature multiplier as a calibrated prediction of transformer FLOP savings; the important agreement is directional: spectral preconditioning helps most in steep-spectrum regimes.

Our findings also connect to recent theory. Prior random-feature and statistical-mechanics analyses show that α\alpha is governed by the data spectrum and target-function structure (Maloney et al., 2022; Bordelon et al., 2024; Bahri et al., 2024); we show that the optimizer also changes the effective spectrum. Bahri et al. (2024) derive scaling exponents from statistical mechanics with a fixed optimizer, while Bergsma et al. (2025) show regularization and data composition can shift α\alpha. Our contribution is complementary: the optimizer preconditioner itself reshapes the effective spectrum. A key caveat is the scale-dependent decay reported by Wen et al. (2025), where Muon/SOAP gains over AdamW shrink from ∼1.4×{\sim}1.4\times at small scales to ∼1.1×{\sim}1.1\times at 1.2B parameters. This suggests the exponent shift may attenuate with feature learning or finite-NN effects; Appendix J discusses these mechanisms.

5 Discussion and Limitations

Practical diagnostic. Our results yield a simple rule: (1) measure your data’s spectral decay from the embedding-covariance eigenvalues; (2) if ss is large, preconditioned optimizers improve α\alpha, not just convergence speed; (3) if ss is small, optimizer choice matters less for scaling.

Falsifiable prediction. Training language models with Muon and AdamW on an artificially flattened-spectrum dataset (e.g., domain-equalized or whitened embeddings) should cause the Muon advantage to shrink or vanish.

Limitations. (1) The random-feature model is lazy and omits feature learning; relative optimizer comparisons should be more robust than absolute α\alpha values. (2) Source exponent bb is fixed at 1.01.0 in the main experiments (see Appendix F for b=2.0b=2.0). (3) Our Muon proxy captures spectral equalization but omits momentum and normalization, and we study width scaling only. (4) The evidence from Wen et al. (2025) suggests the shift may attenuate at scale, which our current framework does not yet explain.

Proposed real-model validation. The direct test is to train GPT-2–scale transformers with AdamW and Muon on standard web text and a spectrum-flattened variant, then fit αMuon−αAdamW\alpha_{\text{Muon}}-\alpha_{\text{AdamW}} across model sizes. This exceeds the present workshop budget; Appendix K gives a concrete protocol.

Future work. Priorities are a closed-form derivation of α⁡(s,b,𝐏)\alpha(s,b,\mathbf{P}), a two-layer feature-learning extension, and the real-model validation above. The framework may also connect to Edge-of-Stability dynamics (Cohen et al., 2021; Kalra et al., 2026).

LLM use disclosure. LLMs were used only for paragraph-level reframing and literature review support.

Appendix B Experimental Details

B.1 Hyperparameters

Table 2 summarizes all optimizer hyperparameters. For iterative optimizers, GD, Diagonal, and Matrix-Sign use deterministic spectral step-size rules, while Sign-GD uses a small candidate search. Weight decay is zero throughout. Training runs for T=2000T=2000 gradient steps; Full NG uses a direct solve (one-step Newton via Cholesky decomposition with Tikhonov regularization λreg=10−6\lambda_{\text{reg}}=10^{-6}), so the step count is irrelevant for that optimizer.

B.2 Fitting Procedure

Scaling exponents are fit by OLS on (log⁡Ni,log⁡Li)(\log N_{i},\log L_{i}) for the five largest model sizes: 200, 500, 1000, 2000, and 5000. We exclude N∈{25,50,100}N\in\{25,50,100\} from the fit because the small-NN regime often deviates from power-law behavior due to finite-size effects. We report the negative regression slope as α\alpha and compute 95% CIs from the standard error of the slope. We verified that the log-log relationship is well approximated by a straight line in this regime (R2>0.95R^{2}>0.95 for all preconditioned optimizers; see Appendix E for details).

B.3 Data Generation

For each configuration (s,N,optimizer,seed)(s,N,\text{optimizer},\text{seed}), we generate:

  1. 1.

    Power-law covariance: Σ=diag⁡(λ1,…,λD)\Sigma=\diag(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{D}) with λi=i−(1+s)\lambda_{i}=i^{-(1+s)}.

  2. 2.

    Training data: rows of XtrainX_{\text{train}} are sampled from 𝒩⁡(0,Σ)\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma). We use a data-rich regime: ntrainn_{\text{train}} is between 10410^{4} and 5×1045{\times}10^{4}, with 20​N20N samples when possible.

  3. 3.

Appendix C Experimental Algorithm

Algorithm 1 provides the complete experimental pipeline in pseudocode. The outer loop sweeps over spectral conditions and model sizes; the inner loop applies each optimizer to the same data realization. This shared-data design ensures that differences in α\alpha are attributable to the optimizer, not to data variation.

Appendix D Derivation Supporting Proposition 1

Proposition 1 is stated as an informal spectral heuristic. A fully rigorous proof would require resolvent-trace analysis of the preconditioned kernel matrix in the proportional-asymptotics limit (in the style of Bordelon et al. 2024), which is beyond this workshop paper’s scope. Here we provide a detailed per-mode convergence-rate argument supporting each of the three claims. The argument is exact for the convergence factors under each preconditioner and heuristic only in the step from mode-wise convergence to the aggregate scaling exponent α\alpha.

D.1 Claim (i): Preconditioning increases α\alpha

In the random-feature model, the test loss decomposes over spectral modes of the data covariance:

L⁡(N)=∑i=1Dℓi​(N),L(N)=\sum_{i=1}^{D}\ell_{i}(N), (1)

where ℓi​(N)\ell_{i}(N) is the residual loss on mode ii (the projection of the target function onto the ii-th eigenvector of Σ\Sigma).

Under GD with learning rate η\eta and training budget TT, the convergence factor for mode ii is:

ciGD=1−(1−η​λ~i)T,c_{i}^{\text{GD}}=1-(1-\eta\tilde{\lambda}_{i})^{T}, (2)

where λ~i\tilde{\lambda}_{i} is the ii-th eigenvalue of the random-feature kernel 𝐅⊤​𝐅/n\mathbf{F}^{\top}\mathbf{F}/n (which concentrates around λi\lambda_{i} in the proportional limit). For the optimal learning rate η∗=2/(λ~1+λ~D)\eta^{*}=2/(\tilde{\lambda}_{1}+\tilde{\lambda}_{D}), modes with large λ~i\tilde{\lambda}_{i} converge exponentially fast while modes with small λ~i\tilde{\lambda}_{i} converge slowly. At a given NN, the number of “well-learned” modes (those with ci≈1c_{i}\approx 1) scales as O⁡(Nγ)O(N^{\gamma}) for some γ<1\gamma<1 that depends on ss and bb, yielding the GD scaling exponent αGD\alpha_{\text{GD}}.

Under full NG (𝐏=(𝐅⊤​𝐅)−1\mathbf{P}=(\mathbf{F}^{\top}\mathbf{F})^{-1}), the preconditioned gradient is (𝐅⊤​𝐅)−1​𝐅⊤​(𝐅𝐚−𝐲)(\mathbf{F}^{\top}\mathbf{F})^{-1}\mathbf{F}^{\top}(\mathbf{F}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{y}), and the convergence factor becomes:

ciNG=1−(1−η)T,c_{i}^{\text{NG}}=1-(1-\eta)^{T}, (3)

which is independent of λ~i\tilde{\lambda}_{i}. All NN modes converge at the same rate, so more modes are well-learned at the same NN, yielding αFullNG>αGD\alpha_{\text{FullNG}}>\alpha_{\text{GD}}.

For Matrix-Sign (𝐏=(𝐅⊤𝐅)−1/2\mathbf{P}=(\mathbf{F}^{\top}\mathbf{F})^{-1/2}), the convergence factor is ciMS=1−(1−η​λ~i/λ~1)Tc_{i}^{\text{MS}}=1-(1-\eta\sqrt{\tilde{\lambda}_{i}}/\sqrt{\tilde{\lambda}_{1}})^{T}—still dependent on λ~i\tilde{\lambda}_{i} but with the eigenvalue range compressed from a ratio of λ~1/λ~D\tilde{\lambda}_{1}/\tilde{\lambda}_{D} to λ~1/λ~D\sqrt{\tilde{\lambda}_{1}/\tilde{\lambda}_{D}} (on a log scale, the dynamic range is halved). This explains why αMatSign≈αFullNG\alpha_{\text{MatSign}}\approx\alpha_{\text{FullNG}} but is sometimes slightly smaller.

D.2 Claim (ii): Δ​α\Delta\alpha is monotone increasing in ss

The key quantity is the effective dynamic range of the eigenvalues seen by the optimizer. For the power-law spectrum λi=i−(1+s)\lambda_{i}=i^{-(1+s)}, the ratio of the largest to the NN-th eigenvalue is:

λ1λN=N1+s.\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{N}}=N^{1+s}. (4)

This ratio grows with both NN and ss. Under GD, this means the convergence factor cNGDc_{N}^{\text{GD}} decreases rapidly with ss—the trailing modes become progressively harder to learn. The fraction of “wasted” capacity (modes that the student can in principle represent but that GD fails to learn in TT steps) is:

Wasted fraction≈1−NeffGDN,\text{Wasted fraction}\approx 1-\frac{N_{\text{eff}}^{\text{GD}}}{N}, (5)

where NeffGDN_{\text{eff}}^{\text{GD}} is the number of modes with ci>1−ϵc_{i}>1-\epsilon for some threshold ϵ\epsilon. Since preconditioning eliminates this waste (achieving NeffNG≈NN_{\text{eff}}^{\text{NG}}\approx N), the gain Δ​α\Delta\alpha is proportional to the wasted fraction, which grows with ss.

D.3 Claim (iii): Δ​α→0\Delta\alpha\to 0 as s→0s\to 0

When s=0s=0, λi=i−1\lambda_{i}=i^{-1}, which is a harmonic spectrum (still decaying but slowly). In the limit s→0s\to 0, λi→1\lambda_{i}\to 1 for all ii (flat spectrum), so ciGD→1−(1−η)Tc_{i}^{\text{GD}}\to 1-(1-\eta)^{T} for all modes. GD already treats all modes equally, and preconditioning adds nothing: αNG=αGD\alpha_{\text{NG}}=\alpha_{\text{GD}}, hence Δ​α=0\Delta\alpha=0.

Connection to known results. Maloney et al. (2022) showed that α\alpha under GD depends on ss and bb through the effective spectral overlap between student and teacher. Our contribution is observing that the preconditioner 𝐏\mathbf{P} modifies this overlap by changing the effective spectrum seen by the optimizer. Prior analyses formalize α\alpha through spectral overlap and redundancy; our work shows this effective redundancy is optimizer-dependent.

Appendix E Power-Law Fit Quality

Table 3 reports R2R^{2} values for all power-law fits. Preconditioned optimizers (Full NG, Matrix-Sign) achieve R2>0.98R^{2}>0.98 across all spectral conditions, confirming that the power-law model is an excellent description of their scaling behavior. GD and Diagonal have lower R2R^{2} at large ss because the scaling curve “bends” as αGD→0\alpha_{\text{GD}}\to 0: the power-law approximation breaks down when the exponent is near zero and finite-size corrections dominate. Sign-GD has poor fit quality at s≥0.75s\geq 0.75 (R2<0.5R^{2}<0.5), reflecting the intrinsic noise of sign-based updates: the sign operation destroys gradient magnitude information, producing high-variance weight trajectories that do not follow a clean power law.

Appendix F Robustness Checks

We verified stability of the main findings to two key hyperparameters that could plausibly affect the α\alpha-shift:

  • •

    Input dimension: D=5000D=5000 (vs. D=1000D=1000). Higher dimension increases the number of spectral modes, potentially changing the effective overlap between student and teacher features. The α\alpha-shift pattern and optimizer ordering are fully preserved (Figure 4a), confirming that our results are not an artifact of the moderate default dimension.

  • •

    Source exponent: b=2.0b=2.0 (vs. b=1.0b=1.0). A steeper teacher coefficient decay concentrates signal energy in fewer modes, changing the effective task difficulty. This changes absolute α\alpha values but preserves the optimizer-dependent shift (Figure 4b), indicating that the preconditioning advantage is robust to the signal structure.

Appendix G Convergence Verification

A potential concern is that the measured α\alpha-shift is merely a convergence artifact: if GD has not converged at 2000 steps, its test loss might be artificially high, inflating the apparent advantage of preconditioned optimizers.

We therefore report convergence diagnostics and interpret the results as finite-budget optimizer-dependent scaling:

1. Comparison to optimal solution. We compare each iterative optimizer’s test loss to the optimal (ridge regression) solution 𝐚∗=(𝐅⊤​𝐅+λreg​I)−1​𝐅⊤​𝐲\mathbf{a}^{*}=(\mathbf{F}^{\top}\mathbf{F}+\lambda_{\text{reg}}I)^{-1}\mathbf{F}^{\top}\mathbf{y} at the same NN. This comparison shows that the reported curves should be interpreted as finite-budget optimizer-dependent scaling curves, not as fully converged ERM curves for every optimizer. For GD, the gap is small only in the easier low-ss, lower-NN cases (for example, about 3.6%3.6\% at s=0.5,N=1000s=0.5,N=1000), and it grows substantially for larger NN and steeper spectra (about 86%86\% at s=1.0,N=5000s=1.0,N=5000). Thus part of the measured advantage is a finite-training-budget effect, which is precisely the regime relevant to optimizer-dependent training dynamics.

2. Direct solve vs. iterative agreement. The Full NG optimizer uses a direct solve (equivalent to infinite gradient steps), yet achieves essentially the same α\alpha as Matrix-Sign (which uses 2000 iterative steps). Their close agreement (Table 1: within about 0.02 across the tested spectra) suggests that strong spectral preconditioning, rather than the exact direct-solve implementation alone, drives the observed ordering. We do not claim to separate convergence speed from finite-budget spectral allocation completely; instead, the result is that optimizer preconditioning changes the finite-budget scaling exponent measured under the stated protocol.

Appendix H Sign-GD Analysis

Sign-GD deserves special discussion as it serves as a negative control—an “adaptive” method that does not improve α\alpha. Unlike the other optimizers, its scaling exponent estimates have very large confidence intervals and poor R2R^{2} (Table 3). This is expected: the sign⁡(⋅)\sign(\cdot) operation discards gradient magnitude information, so each update step has magnitude η\eta regardless of the true gradient scale. This produces:

  1. 1.

    High variance across random seeds: the stochastic trajectory is very sensitive to initialization because Sign-GD cannot distinguish between large and small gradient components.

  2. 2.

    Poor power-law fits: the noisy loss trajectory yields high residual variance in the (log⁡N,log⁡L)(\log N,\log L) regression.

  3. 3.

    No scaling improvement: effective α\alpha values are close to (or slightly below) GD, confirming that the sign operation provides no useful spectral preconditioning.

The inclusion of Sign-GD strengthens our mechanistic story: the key mechanism is spectral equalization (reweighting per-mode convergence rates), not merely “adaptivity” in a generic sense. Sign-GD is adaptive (it adjusts update directions) but does not equalize spectral modes, and correspondingly does not improve α\alpha.

Appendix I Interpretation Caveats

We highlight several caveats important for interpreting our results in the context of real neural network training.

Lazy vs. rich regime. The random-feature model operates in the “lazy” regime where features are fixed and only the top-layer weights are learned. Real neural networks operate in the “rich” or feature-learning regime, where the representation itself adapts during training. Feature learning could either amplify or dampen the α\alpha-shift. On one hand, preconditioned optimizers might enable more effective feature learning, amplifying the advantage. On the other hand, feature learning might naturally mitigate the spectral imbalance that GD suffers from, reducing the need for explicit preconditioning (Yang et al., 2024). The conflicting empirical evidence—substantial Muon advantages at moderate scale (Chen et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025) but attenuation at 1.2B parameters (Wen et al., 2025)—suggests that feature learning may increasingly substitute for preconditioning at scale. See Appendix J for extended discussion.

Width vs. depth scaling. Our model studies width scaling (NN random features) with no notion of depth. Depth scaling involves qualitatively different phenomena—vanishing/exploding gradients, residual connections, and layer-wise feature hierarchies—that may interact with preconditioning in ways not captured here.

Compute multiplier interpretation. The “effective compute multiplier” (Figure 3) should be interpreted as the factor by which GD must increase model size to match preconditioned loss, not as a direct FLOPs comparison. Real preconditioned optimizers (Shampoo, Muon) incur per-step overhead from computing the preconditioner. The total wall-clock advantage therefore depends on the amortized cost of preconditioning relative to the α\alpha-shift benefit.

Absolute vs. relative α\alpha values. The absolute values of α\alpha in our random-feature model differ from those measured in real language model training (where α≈0.05\alpha\approx 0.05–0.10.1 for loss scaling with parameters). We caution against interpreting our absolute α\alpha values as predictions for real models. The relative comparisons—the ordering of optimizers and the broad increase of the preconditioning advantage with spectral steepness, up to saturation—are the robust predictions.

Appendix J Scale-Dependent Decay of the Optimizer Advantage

The results of Wen et al. (2025) present the most important challenge to a simple “exponent shift” narrative. They train language models from 25M to 1.2B parameters with Muon, SOAP, and AdamW, and find that the compute multiplier decreases with model size—from approximately 1.4×1.4\times at 100M to approximately 1.1×1.1\times at 1.2B. If the α\alpha-shift from our random-feature model (Proposition 1) transferred directly and remained constant, we would expect the multiplier to grow with NN, not shrink.

We discuss four mechanisms—not mutually exclusive—that could reconcile these findings with our framework.

(a) Finite-NN corrections and pre-asymptotic behavior. Our Proposition 1 describes the asymptotic scaling exponent. In practice, finite-NN effects generate curvature in the (log⁡N,log⁡L)(\log N,\log L) plot, and the local exponent at any particular NN can differ from the asymptotic value. In our own simulations, the α\alpha-shift measured from the smallest model sizes (N<200N<200) differs from the asymptotic fit—this is why we exclude N<200N<200 from our fits. For real LLMs, the “asymptotic” regime may require scales beyond 1.2B, particularly if the effective number of learnable spectral modes is much smaller than the parameter count.

(b) Feature learning reduces spectral imbalance. Our model operates in the lazy (kernel) regime where features are fixed. Real networks operate in the rich regime where features co-adapt with the loss landscape. As models grow larger, feature learning becomes more powerful (Yang et al., 2024) and may naturally re-weight the effective spectrum seen by the optimizer—partially “self-preconditioning” the gradient. If feature learning achieves some of the spectral equalization that an explicit preconditioner provides, the marginal benefit of Muon/SOAP would decline at scale, consistent with the Wen et al. (2025) findings.

(c) Effective spectrum changes with scale. The spectral exponent ss of the data covariance is not fixed across model sizes: larger models trained on more tokens may encounter effectively different spectral distributions. If larger models see a flatter effective spectrum (lower ss)—for example because broader data mixtures or longer training equilibrate representations—then our framework predicts a smaller Δ​α\Delta\alpha (Proposition 1(ii)), exactly the attenuation observed.

(d) Benchmark and implementation differences. The Chen et al. (2025) result (∼1.4×{\sim}1.4\times) uses carefully scaled optimizer hyperparameters, while Wen et al. (2025) use a different evaluation and tuning protocol. AdamW performance is notoriously sensitive to learning rate scheduling and weight decay at scale; differences in how well each study tunes the AdamW baseline can shift the measured speedup by 0.20.2–0.3×0.3\times.

Our assessment. We believe explanations (a) and (b) are most likely to be dominant, and that the true picture involves a scale-dependent α\alpha-shift: the exponent improvement is real at moderate scale, but attenuates—possibly to zero—as feature learning and finite-NN corrections become important. Our random-feature framework captures the “starting point” of this phenomenon (the existence and spectral-dependence of the shift) but not its scale-dependent decay, which requires a feature-learning extension. We view this as the most important theoretical open problem that our work highlights.

Appendix K Proposed Real-Model Validation Protocol

We describe a concrete experiment to test our falsifiable prediction in the LLM setting.

Setup.

  • •

    Models: GPT-2–architecture transformers at 4 sizes: 125M, 350M, 760M, 1.3B parameters, using μ\muP (Yang et al., 2022) for hyperparameter transfer.

  • •

    Optimizers: AdamW (baseline) and Muon, with learning rates transferred via μ\muP.

  • •

    Data: FineWeb-Edu (standard, s≈1.0s\approx 1.0) and a spectrum-flattened variant created by equalizing domain proportions and/or applying PCA whitening to embedding inputs.

  • •

    Training: Chinchilla-optimal token counts at each size (Hoffmann et al., 2022).

  • •

    Evaluation: Final validation loss on a held-out split.

Analysis. Fit α\alpha separately for each (optimizer, dataset) pair by OLS on (log⁡N,log⁡L)(\log N,\log L) across the 4 model sizes. The predictions to test:

  1. 1.

    αMuon>αAdamW\alpha_{\text{Muon}}>\alpha_{\text{AdamW}} on standard data (positive Δ​α\Delta\alpha).

  2. 2.

    Δ​α\Delta\alpha is smaller on spectrum-flattened data than on standard data (spectral dependence).

  3. 3.

    The magnitude of Δ​α\Delta\alpha may attenuate with scale, consistent with Wen et al. (2025).

Compute requirements. 2​ optimizers×2​ datasets×4​ sizes=162\text{ optimizers}\times 2\text{ datasets}\times 4\text{ sizes}=16 training runs. At Chinchilla-optimal tokens, this requires approximately 4×10194\times 10^{19} FLOPs total (∼80{\sim}80 A100-hours for the 1.3B runs, ∼120{\sim}120 A100-hours total). This is substantial but feasible for a well-resourced follow-up; it exceeds the budget for this workshop submission.

Appendix L Code Availability

All simulation code and analysis scripts will be made available in an anonymous repository upon publication. Experiments were run on Modal cloud compute with CPU containers (no GPU required). Total compute cost: approximately 2 hours of wall-clock time on 300+ parallel containers, totaling roughly 600 CPU-hours. The entire experiment suite can be reproduced for under $20 in cloud compute.
